opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to start is to step back and ask what a "patient representation" even means. Traditionally in medicine, a patient is represented as a collection of fairly disconnected things: lab values, diagnoses, codes in an electronic health record, maybe an imaging scan, maybe a genome if you're lucky. Each of those is analyzed in its own silo. What we're trying to do with the virtual cell idea is go bottom-up, and say: a lot of what's going on with a patient ultimately comes down to what's happening in their cells, how genes, proteins, and pathways interact, and how cells respond to perturbations like drugs or disease.

So the way I think about it is in layers. At the lowest level you want a model that understands cellular state. You train it on large amounts of single-cell data, transcriptomics, perturbation screens, and so on, so it learns a representation where a cell's state is an embedding, and you can ask what happens to that cell if I knock out this gene or apply this compound. That's the virtual cell part: a model you can query and simulate with, rather than just a lookup table of measurements.

Then the question is how you go from cells to a patient. A patient is essentially a population of cells across tissues, in a particular context. So you aggregate: you represent the tissue as a collection of cell states and their interactions, and the patient as a composition of those, combined with the clinical context, history, and other modalities. This is where a lot of my background in graphs and relational learning comes in. Biology is fundamentally relational. Genes interact with genes, cells communicate with cells, and patients connect to diagnoses, treatments, and outcomes. Representing all of that as one large heterogeneous graph and learning over it lets information flow between levels, so the patient representation is grounded in molecular mechanism rather than just being correlational features from a health record.

Why does that matter? A couple of reasons. One is generalization. If your representation is grounded in mechanism, you have a better shot at reasoning about patients or treatments you haven't seen much of, like rare diseases, where you'll never have enough patients to learn purely from the data. The second is interpretability and actionability. If the model says this patient is likely to respond to a drug, you'd like to trace that back to which pathway, which cell type, which perturbation is driving it. That's much more useful to a clinician or a drug developer than a black-box score.

And honestly, the hard parts are still very open. Data is heterogeneous and noisy, the lab-to-patient gap is real, since cell lines don't behave like cells in a human body, and evaluation is tricky: how do you know your virtual cell is actually right and not just fitting the benchmarks? So I see this as a long-term research program. But the overall vision is a foundation-model-like representation that spans molecules, cells, tissues, and patients, where you can simulate and ask counterfactual questions, and that's what I think could really change how we do precision medicine.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so thanks for having me, Sam. Maybe let me start one level below the patient, because the way we think about it, the patient is really the top of a hierarchy, and the cell is the fundamental unit. So the idea behind the virtual cell is: can we build a model, a representation, of a cell that is general enough that we can ask it questions. What happens if I knock out this gene? What happens if I expose this cell to this drug? What happens if I change the environment around the cell? And the exciting thing is that in the last few years, the experimental technologies have gotten to the point where we can actually measure this at scale. Single-cell sequencing, Perturb-seq, spatial transcriptomics, imaging. We now have hundreds of millions of cells that have been measured, and we have data where people have systematically perturbed cells and observed what happened. So for the first time, there is the kind of data that you need to train a model that is not just descriptive, but predictive.

And the way we approach it is very much in the spirit of foundation models. We don't want to build one model for one cell type or one disease. We want to learn an embedding of a cell, a representation, from a very large and heterogeneous collection of data, and then that representation should transfer. You should be able to take a cell you've never seen before, from a tissue you've never seen, and the model should have a reasonable prior about how that cell will behave. In some sense, the analogy to language models is pretty direct. The "tokens" are genes and their expression levels, and the "context" is the state of the cell, its environment, its neighbors in a tissue.

Now, how do you get from there to a patient? A patient is not one cell, it's trillions of cells, organized into tissues and organs, interacting with each other. So what we are really building is a hierarchy. You have representations of molecules, of cells, of tissues, and then the patient is a composition of those. And this is where my background in graphs and networks comes in, because the natural way to represent this is relational. Cells talk to each other, tissues are organized spatially, and you want a model that respects that structure rather than flattening everything into one vector.

The part I find most compelling is that this gives you a way to do in-silico experiments. Today, if you want to know whether a drug works, you run a clinical trial, which is expensive, slow, and often fails. If we have a good enough virtual cell, and eventually a virtual patient, you could first run the experiment in the model, narrow down the hypotheses, and only then go to the wet lab or to the clinic. I don't think we're there yet, to be clear. The models still get a lot of things wrong, especially out of distribution. But the trajectory is really encouraging, and the community is starting to coordinate around benchmarks and shared data, which I think is what it will take.

astra-6.text:
I think about it from the bottom up. A patient is a very complex biological system, so the question is how we build representations that connect what is happening at the molecular and cellular level to what we observe clinically.

With an AI virtual cell, the idea is to learn a representation of a cell that captures its state and its context, but also allows us to predict how it would respond to a change. What happens if we perturb a gene, introduce a drug, or change the environment? We want to move from describing a cell to predicting its behavior.

Then the challenge is connecting those scales. Cells interact with other cells, they form tissues, and those tissues operate within a patient. A representation of a patient would need to capture that organization, alongside information about their disease and treatment history. It’s not simply an average of their cells.

The longer-term ambition is to use those representations to reason about interventions: why might two patients with the same diagnosis respond differently to the same treatment? That’s the direction we want to go, but building a useful cell model and connecting it to patient-level outcomes are distinct challenges.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that a patient is not just a single vector. There are many levels of organization, from molecules to cells to tissues and organs, and ultimately the whole patient. What we would like to do with the AI Virtual Cell is build representations that connect those levels.

At the cellular level, you want a representation that captures the state of a cell, but also its context: What tissue is it in? What other cells surround it? How are they interacting? Then the question becomes how to bring those cellular representations together with the measurements and clinical information we have about a patient.

And the goal is to go beyond describing the current state. Can we predict how that state would change under a perturbation—a drug, for example? If we can connect the effect of an intervention on cells to its consequences for the patient, then we have a representation that is useful for reasoning about disease and treatment.
